statement: A circle does not touch a circle at more points than one, whether it touch it internally or externally.
heath_proof: For, if possible, let the circle ABDC touch the circle EBFD, first internally, at morepoints than one, namely D, B. Let the centre G of the circle ABDC, and the centre H of EBFD, be taken. Therefore the straight linejoined from G to H will fall on B, D. [III. 11] Let it so fall, as BGHD. Then, since the point G is the centre of the circle ABCD,BG is equal to GD;  therefore BG is greater than HD; therefore BH is much greater than HD. Again, since the point H is the centre of the circle EBFD,BH is equal to HD;  but it was also proved much greater than it: which is impossible. Therefore a circle does not touch a circle internally at more points than one. I say further that neither does it so touch it externally. For, if possible, let the circle ACK touch the circle ABDC at more points than one, namely A, C, and let AC be joined. Then, since on the circumference of each of the circlesABDC, ACK two points A, C have been taken at random, the straight line joining the points will fall within each circle; [III. 2] but it fell within the circle ABCD and outside ACK [III. Def. 3]: which is absurd. Therefore a circle does not touch a circle externally at more points than one. And it was proved that neither does it so touch it internally.
ai_proof_text:
3.13
**Statement:** A circle does not touch a circle at more points than one, whether it touch it internally or externally.

**Step 1.** Suppose, if possible, that the circle ABDC touches the circle EBFD internally at more points than one, say at the points B and D. Let G be the centre of the circle ABDC and H the centre of the circle EBFD (3.1).

**Step 2.** Since the two circles touch one another internally, the straight line joining their centres G and H, when produced, falls on the point of contact (3.11). As both B and D are points of contact, the straight line GH produced passes through both B and D; hence the points B, G, H, D all lie on one straight line.

**Step 3.** This straight line, drawn through the centre G and produced in both directions, is terminated by the circumference of the circle ABDC at B and D, so that BD is a diameter of the circle ABDC and G lies between B and D (D1.17); in the same way BD is a diameter of the circle EBFD and H lies between B and D. Moreover, since the circles touch one another, G and H are not the same point (3.6). Thus G and H are two distinct points of BD, each lying between B and D; let H be the one nearer to D, so that the points lie in the order B, G, H, D. (If G is the nearer, the same reasoning applies with the roles of the two circles interchanged.)

**Step 4.** Since G is the centre of the circle ABDC and the points B, D lie on its circumference, BG is equal to GD (D1.15).

**Step 5.** Since H lies between G and D, HD is a part of GD; therefore GD is greater than HD (CN5). Hence, by Step 4, BG is greater than HD.

**Step 6.** Since G lies between B and H, BG is a part of BH; therefore BH is greater than BG (CN5). Consequently BH is much greater than HD.

**Step 7.** But H is the centre of the circle EBFD and the points B, D lie on its circumference; therefore BH is equal to HD (D1.15). This contradicts Step 6. Therefore a circle does not touch a circle internally at more points than one.

**Step 8.** Next suppose, if possible, that the circle ACK touches the circle ABDC externally at more points than one, say at the points A and C. Join AC (P1).

**Step 9.** Since the points A and C lie on the circumference of the circle ABDC, the straight line AC joining them falls within the circle ABDC (3.2).

**Step 10.** Likewise, since the points A and C lie on the circumference of the circle ACK, the straight line AC falls within the circle ACK (3.2).

**Step 11.** But the circles touch one another externally: they meet without cutting one another (D3.3), and each lies wholly outside the other, so that whatever falls within the circle ABDC falls outside the circle ACK. Hence AC, which by Step 9 falls within the circle ABDC, falls outside the circle ACK. This contradicts Step 10. Therefore a circle does not touch a circle externally at more points than one.

**Step 12.** Therefore a circle does not touch a circle at more points than one, whether it touch it internally or externally. Q.E.D.
